facts.statement: Global evolution of central banks (courseware): the primary stimulus for establishing central banks and strengthening their activities in many parts of the world in the twentieth century emanated from the exigency of war financing; economic historians point out that war finance was the prime consideration for the constitution of many early central banks, and war financing also led to nationalisation of many central banks which till then were functioning as private entities. Once the spectre of war receded, central banks focused increasingly on mobilising resources for planned development and on tackling high inflation. In the initial years of existence central banks performed minimal functions like being the lender of last resort and in most countries were also given the monopoly of bank note issue, because when multiple organisations issued notes, controlling the quantity, quality and acceptability of currency was difficult; for maintaining stability in the internal value of money the monopoly of note issue should be the exclusive prerogative of the central bank. Central banks also came to shoulder the responsibility of maintaining a stable external value of money (the rate at which the value of domestic currency is expressed in terms of foreign currency) so as to maintain a stable exchange rate to facilitate international trade and commerce. The history of central banking goes back to the seventeenth century when Riksbank in Sweden was established as a central bank in 1668 (courseware) and recognised as the first central bank in the world; set up as a joint stock bank, it was chartered to lend funds to the Government and to act as a clearing house for commerce; later it abandoned commercial lending and was endowed with the function of monopoly of note issue in 1897. Several central banks such as the Bank of England and Banque de France were set up with private capital, helped sovereigns finance their debt and were engaged in banking activities. In the nineteenth century, several countries in Europe such as France (1800), Finland (1811), the Netherlands (1814), Austria (1816), Norway (1816), Denmark (1818), Portugal (1846), Belgium (1850), Spain (1874), Germany (1876), Italy (1893) and Japan in Asia (1882) established central banks. Central banks initially took the responsibility of developing the financial system in line with the financial requirements of the country; the financial infrastructure widened, and central banks started managing payment and settlement systems, as finality of settlement of transactions rests with the central banks. Because of financial institution failures and the need for resolution of crisis situations, central banks came to shoulder greater regulatory and supervisory roles, and started risk management systems aimed at regulating and supervising the financial system. In many developing countries, including India, with the emergence of nation states after the disappearance of colonial regimes, central bank mandates transcended well beyond typical central banking functions to encompass wide developmental pursuits such as economic recovery and promoting growth; this entrusted the banks with greater responsibility of economic development but exposed them to the threat of fiscal dominance. In the late twentieth century, monetary policy formulation assumed critical importance; concerns about inflation, financial stability and risk management, global financial markets and crises have brought price stability, financial stability and risk management to the fore.

Country histories (courseware): the Bank of England was founded in 1694 in the premises of Threadneedle Street, acted as the government bank and the UK central bank, issued bank notes, controlled the UK gold reserves and, since 1997, sets official interest rates; it is the second oldest central bank in the world after the Swedish Riksbank (founded 1668). William Paterson, a Scotsman, noticed that the nation finances were in disarray and had no real system of money or credit; he had a successful scheme in which 1.2 million pounds was loaned to the government from funds raised by subscribers who, in return, were incorporated into the company of the Bank of England. The Bank was initially established as an agency for conduct of commercial banking operations, accepting deposits and issuing notes, securing large government accounts and becoming the government banker and debt manager; it survived the South Sea Bubble crash of the 1720s when smaller banks went to it to be bailed out, so playing the lender of last resort function; with the renewal of the Charter in 1791 it was described as the public exchequer and acted as the bankers bank; in 1844 the Bank Charter Act granted the Bank a monopoly to print bank notes in England and Wales; during the First World War it played a major role in managing the government borrowing; it was nationalised in 1946 and in 1997 Gordon Brown, then the chancellor, effectively delegated to the Bank operational independence to set interest rates. The Bank of France (Banque de France), headquartered in Paris, was established in the year 1800, founded partly with state funds but mainly with private capital; the French government retained a say through the appointment of the Governor and two Deputy Governors, while shareholders were represented by a board of 15 regents elected by the 200 largest shareholders; it was initially granted the exclusive privilege to issue bank notes in Paris for a period of 15 years, later authorised to establish discount offices in towns where commercial requirements made this necessary and subsequently the privilege of note issue was extended to cover the whole of France in 1848 because of the transformation of nine provincial banks with note issuing powers into branches of the Bank; the Bank was nationalised in 1946, statutes in 1973 placed greater power with the Bank general council, and the Bank gained independence in 1993 to ensure price stability; it entered the European System of Central Banks in 1999 when the Euro became the single currency. The Banco de Portugal was established as a public limited company in 1846, a note issuing commercial bank. In Germany, the Bundesbank was established in 1957 under the Bundesbank Law, its predecessor, known as the Reichsbank, operated from 1876 to 1945; the Bundesbank was a federal central bank that gradually helped integrate its separate units, expected to integrate the multiple settings and existing regulations across Germany; it is now a part of the European System of Central Banks. The Bank of Italy was founded in 1893 as part of the reorganisation of the Italian banking and monetary system that had reached near collapse at the beginning of the 1890s; its fundamental task was to rid itself from the problems inherited and restore a capital base, and it is now a part of the European System of Central Banks. The Federal Reserve System (the Fed) is the central banking system of the United States, established in 1913 following the enactment of the Federal Reserve Act, in response to a series of financial panics (particularly the panic of 1907) that showed the need for central bank to avert such crises. Federal Reserve key objectives for monetary policy: maximising employment, stabilising prices and moderating long-term interest rates (the first two objectives are referred to as the Fed dual mandate); the Fed later performed supervisory and regulatory functions, maintaining the stability of the financial system and providing financial services to depository institutions, the US Government and foreign official institutions. Structure: the Board of Governors (seven members nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate, each serving a full term of fourteen years, one term beginning on 1 February of even-numbered years, with the Chair and Vice Chair also named by the President from among the members and confirmed by the Senate), the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) of twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks located in major cities and various advisory councils; the FOMC sets monetary policy and consists of all seven members of the Board of Governors and the twelve regional bank presidents, though only five presidents vote at any given time: the president of the New York Fed and four others rotate on one-year terms. The Fed considers itself independent because its monetary policy decisions do not have to be approved by the President or anyone else in the executive or legislative branches, it does not receive funding appropriated by the Congress, and the terms of the members of the Board of Governors span multiple presidential and congressional terms. The US Government receives all of the system profits after a statutory dividend of 6 per cent on member banks capital investment is paid and a surplus is maintained.

Evolution of central bank functions (courseware): while each country has a unique evolution of its central bank, there are some common features: whenever central banks were set up to tackle similar problems their institutional structures were similar; with the onset of the First World War, paper money issued by central banks replaced the full value metal coin money. As notes became legal tender and ceased to be convertible into gold, the power of central banks over money supply and price stabilisation policies became feasible; after the First World War the role of supervising the business of private commercial banks was added and lender of last resort function strengthened during financial panics; the war also led to central banks increasing involvement in extending credit to governments and to handling government debt; central banks were allowed to trade government paper in the open market and were entitled to develop open market policy instruments for fine-tuning of interest rates and for credit and money supply expansion; since 1933 in the US and shortly after the Second World War in Germany, central banks were empowered to impose the stipulation of maintenance of minimum reserve requirements by banks, an important direct tool of monetary management. As financial systems developed, central banks reoriented their policies and strengthened their roles to cope with the new challenges; during global crises such as the Great Depression of the 1930s, the mandate given to most central banks included monetary stability, promotion of full employment and maximisation of growth. Functions can be broadly categorised into monetary policy functions, banker to the banks, banker to the government and developmental functions; the functions of note issue and maintenance of internal and external value of currency evolved as the key functional areas of central banking; the responsibility of promoting growth was subsequently added to it. With the development of the financial sector, the lender-of-last-resort function assumed significance and central banks strengthened supervisory and regulatory roles; with renewed emphasis on financial stability as an additional objective of monetary policy, supervisory and regulatory functions received further impetus; many central banks were originally established predominantly to finance the activities of their governments, and this function has been reviewed and many central banks have ceased to finance their governments in recent years. Central banks also assumed new functions that focus on development of markets, institutions and communication policies. Most central banks act as bankers to their respective governments; in times of war finance received utmost importance; dependence of governments on central banks exerted immense pressure on the conduct of monetary policy. The lender of last resort function faces the moral hazard problem: it arises from the expectation that the banking system maintaining a complacent behaviour in managing its balance sheet in the expectation that it would be getting central bank support in case of a solvency or liquidity problem; to discourage such behaviour central banks often subject the affected bank to rigorous scrutiny of its balance sheet and also extend any support only at a penal rate of interest; the financial system also faces systemic risks in the wake of bank failures. Central banks also realised the close relationship between financial development and economic development, and so credit policy formulation assumed paramount relevance; central banks play a pivotal role in steering the process of financial development through institution building, and simultaneously put in place policy and institutional mechanisms that help in circumscribing the inherent risks.

Reasons for proliferation and conflicting roles (courseware): evolution of central banking is essentially a twentieth century phenomenon as there were only about a dozen central banks in the world at the turn of the nineteenth century, but at present there are more than 160 central banks (courseware count). Banking became more complex and the financial sector formed an integral part of the economy over time; with the plethora of bank failures and the increasing concern of depositors about the safety and security of their funds, the need for appropriate regulation surfaced; as central banks essentially emerged as a nation state phenomenon, they proliferated as nation states themselves emerged and multiplied. The reasons for the origin and proliferation of central banks: the need for an appropriate authority to be entrusted with the function of note issue; the need for an agency to act as a banker and lender to the government; and the need for an agency to regulate and supervise the banking and financial entities and to serve as a lender of last resort to banks. Conflicting roles: the role of a central bank as banker to the government gained renewed relevance particularly in times of war; the current professional thinking is that the role of a central bank as a debt manager of government conflicts with the core objective of central bank, namely price stability; many central banks pursue price stability as a major objective of monetary policy; as debt manager, it was observed that central banks financed government deficits partly, and extending credit to government puts pressure on monetary policy as central banks need to create excess money to meet government needs; this is fraught with the problem of generating inflationary pressures. This has led to the view that central banks should be independent of government and should divest themselves of their role as debt managers. Central bank independence gained thrust after the Vietnam war in the 1960s and 1970s, the expansion of world liquidity and the ensuing enduring inflation; the undue fiscal and monetary expansion in Latin America gave further impetus to the view that the central bank should be independent of any government interference; as a result inflation targeting has emerged as the principal objective of central banks in many countries, with central banks independently pursuing an inflation target and being accountable for maintaining inflation within a pre-assigned band. Another view is that central banks should not abandon their parents (the sovereign government) and come of age; instances like the case of two currencies in Iraq in the 1990s and that of the Bank of Japan in recent years provide a contrary view to the come-of-age hypothesis. Another issue relating to central banks role is that of its function of regulation and supervision of the financial entities: this issue arises in the wake of the observation that the roles of a regulator and supervisor are different and entrusting these roles to a single authority, namely the central bank, can lead to conflict of interest; this draws an analogy to the doctrine of separation of powers propounded by Montesquieu which assigns distinct roles to the law enactment authority and law implementing authority; accordingly, it was felt that the supervisory authority should be outside the realm of central banks; this view has gained considerable strength in the UK with the establishment of the Financial Services Authority (FSA) in 2000; several other countries followed suit thereafter; in India, however, the Board for Financial Supervision (BFS) functions within the ambit of the Reserve Bank as an apex level supervisory authority. A new objective, financial stability, is also assigned to central banks beyond price stability; historically price stability along with maintaining external value of currency was achieved through the mechanics of the Gold Standard and later through the dollar anchor and its relation to gold; the world lost its monetary anchor on 15 August 1971 when the US decided to delink the dollar from gold; since then countries have been experimenting with several types of monetary anchors for maintaining the stability of the external value of currency and the search for a new anchor continues. The core of modern central banking also consists of development of financial markets and institutions, financial regulation and supervision, management of government debt, administration of payment and settlement systems and maintenance of the external value of currency; though many central banks have adopted inflation targeting as the core objective and recorded a fair degree of success, the consensus on inflation targeting as an exclusive central bank mandate remains elusive.

Central banks in developed and developing countries (courseware): there are marked differences in the development of central bank functions as between developed and developing countries. The developed countries are characterised by a well-diversified and strong financial super structure; they are advanced in the sense of both financial widening and financial deepening; hence the monetary transmission processes of central banks are smooth and fast, and policy signals are transmitted quickly; any change in interest rates by banks in advanced economies triggers an immediate response from the banking system and the financial markets and sets the move for reallocation of resources; for example, for a greater part of the period from 1970 through October 1979 the Federal Reserve relied on the federal funds rate (the rate that banks charge one another on overnight loans of reserves) as its operating target in seeking to attain its monetary objectives, the objective being to equalise the demand for and supply of reserves at the desired rate. In the developed countries there is a preponderant use of cheques and drafts rather than currency as a means of payment, so the currency-management of the central bank tends to be minimal as compared to developing countries; in developing countries currency forms a major proportion of money supply and a vast majority of the population use currency as a means of payment; the currency to deposit ratio is generally very high in developing countries (as high as 80 per cent in some) as compared with less than 10 per cent in developed markets; currency management becomes complex and intricate. The developing countries are characterised by poor financial infrastructure and the banking network is sparsely spread, so central banks of such countries need to expend efforts at creating financial infrastructure for channelising savings for investment purposes. In developing countries central banks face the problem of existence of informal markets; a significant part of economic activity springs from these informal markets which operate independently of the organised money market, weakening the monetary transmission process, as interest rate signals from the central bank generally do not affect the operations of informal markets; even within the organised financial segment, in view of the weak financial structure, policy signals from the central bank are not fully realised, so monetary policy transmission is somewhat weak. In industrial countries the main role for which central banks were formed was that of lender-of-the-last-resort; as against this, central banks in developing countries like India came into existence to promote the spread of commercial banks and other channels of credit flow; the principal reason for the genesis of central banks in several developing countries is that they should primarily play a developmental role. There is a marked difference between central banks of older developing countries and those in transition economies: the older developing countries developed their systems gradually, while transition economies have the benefit of being late comers and learn from the experience of other countries; central banks in these economies were able to start on a clean slate and successfully graft systems from developed countries, while older developing countries needed frameworks compatible with existing systems; merely grafting developed country models may not be suitable and the framework needs to be tailored to specific features. In developing countries the central banks acted on two separate levels: first, they had to rely more on direct or sector specific tools in the conduct of monetary policy; second, they needed to develop financial markets and then move to market based instruments, and function under conditions of inadequate or no autonomy, i.e., under conditions of fiscal dominance. The role of central banks in developing countries is often that of a facilitator who fosters development of the financial markets not only to facilitate the process of smooth monetary transmission but also to meet the financial needs of the governments and to achieve the socio-economic goals of the country. The global financial crisis of 2008 led to redefining the mandate of central banks, and the Covid-19 pandemic showed an unprecedented health shock that has simultaneously affected demand, supply and financial conditions, with central banks reacting strongly using a range of measures to shore up financial markets and mitigate the adverse economic impact.

payload.title: Why and how central banks emerged
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Main stimulus:** the **need to finance wars**. Many early central banks were set up (and later **nationalised**) for **war finance**; after war, they turned to **mobilising resources for development** and **fighting inflation**.

**First functions:** **lender of last resort** and **monopoly of note issue** (one issuer makes the **quantity, quality and acceptability** of currency controllable and protects the **internal value of money**). Central banks also took charge of the **external value of money** (the exchange rate) to support **trade**.

**Early history (as the courseware states):** **Riksbank (Sweden, 1668)** is treated as the **first central bank** (a joint stock bank lending to the Government; **note issue monopoly in 1897**); the **Bank of England** and **Banque de France** were set up with **private capital** and helped sovereigns **finance their debt**. Nineteenth century bank dates: **France 1800**, **Finland 1811**, **Netherlands 1814**, **Austria and Norway 1816**, **Denmark 1818**, **Portugal 1846**, **Belgium 1850**, **Spain 1874**, **Germany 1876**, **Italy 1893**, **Japan 1882**.

**Widening role:** developing the **financial system**, **payment and settlement systems** (central banks provide **finality of settlement**), then **regulation and supervision** after bank failures, plus **risk management**. In **developing countries** (including India) post-colonial mandates grew to **development**, raising the risk of **fiscal dominance**. From the late twentieth century **price stability, financial stability and risk management** came to the fore.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: War finance explains why many central banks started as government bankers.

payload.title: How the functions of central banks evolved
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Milestones:** **paper money** issued by central banks replaced **full-value coins** around **World War I**; once notes were **legal tender** and **not convertible into gold**, central banks could control **money supply and prices**. After WWI they took on **supervision of commercial banks**, a firmer **lender of last resort** role, **credit to governments** and **debt management**, and used **open market operations** to fine-tune **interest rates and money supply**. Since **1933 (US)** and soon after **WWII (Germany)** central banks could impose **minimum reserve requirements**.

**Crises changed mandates:** the **Great Depression** added **monetary stability, full employment and growth**. Functions group into **monetary policy**, **banker to banks**, **banker to government** and **developmental** functions; **note issue and internal and external value of currency** are the key areas, with **growth promotion** added later.

**Financial stability** became an added objective, so **supervisory functions** grew; many central banks have **stopped financing their governments**.

**Moral hazard in last resort lending:** banks may behave **complacently** expecting **rescue**; central banks counter with **rigorous scrutiny** and by lending **at a penal rate**.

**Development role:** because **financial and economic development go together**, central banks run **credit policy**, **build institutions** and put in place **mechanisms to contain risks** from financial deepening.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Each crisis added a function: supervision after bank panics, reserve requirements after inflation, and stability after the 2008 crisis.

payload.title: Reasons for proliferation and conflicting roles
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Growth in number:** only about **a dozen** central banks in **1800**, but **over 160** now (courseware count). Reasons: **banking became complex**, **bank failures** made **regulation** necessary, and central banks **spread with nation states**.

**Why a central bank exists:** (1) an authority to run **note issue**; (2) an agency to be **banker and lender to the government**; (3) an agency to **regulate and supervise financial entities** and be **lender of last resort**.

**Conflicts of role:**

- **Banker or debt manager to Government vs price stability:** lending to the Government means **creating money**, risking **inflation**. This supports **central bank independence**, strengthened after the **Vietnam war** inflation and the **Latin American** episodes; **inflation targeting** (an **independent** bank pursuing a **target band**) became the main objective in many countries. A competing 'come of age' debate says central banks should not drop their 'parent', the **sovereign Government**.
- **Regulator and supervisor roles:** possible **conflict of interest**; by analogy with **Montesquieu's separation of powers** some countries moved supervision out of the central bank (the **UK Financial Services Authority, 2000**); in **India** the **Board for Financial Supervision** works **within the Reserve Bank**.

**Anchors:** price stability and the **external value** of currency relied on the **Gold Standard** and then the **dollar anchor**; the world lost its **anchor** on **15 August 1971** when the **US delinked the dollar from gold**.

**Modern core:** **development of financial markets and institutions**, **regulation and supervision**, **government debt management**, **payment and settlement systems** and the **external value** of currency; consensus that **inflation targeting** should be the **sole mandate** is **lacking**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The debate between independence and development roles shapes how each country designs its central bank.

payload.title: Central banks in developed and developing countries
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Feature | Developed countries | Developing countries |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Financial structure** | **Diversified and strong**; both **widening and deepening** | **Poor infrastructure**, **sparse banking network** |
| **Transmission** | **Smooth and fast**; interest rate changes pass through quickly | **Weak**; **informal markets** do not respond to policy signals |
| **Payments** | Mostly **cheques and drafts**; **currency to deposit ratio below about 10 per cent** | **Currency dominates**; **ratio as high as 80 per cent** in some; currency management is complex |
| **Origin of central bank** | Mainly **lender of last resort** | To **promote spread of commercial banks and credit flow**: a **developmental role** |
| **Instruments** | **Market based** (for example the **federal funds rate** as operating target 1970-79) | More **direct, sector specific tools** at first; must **develop financial markets** |
| **Autonomy** | High | Often limited, with **fiscal dominance** |

**Old vs transition economies:** transition economies can **start on a clean slate** and **graft systems** from developed countries; older developing countries must fit new frameworks to **existing systems**; a model must be **tailored to country features**.

**Role in developing countries:** a **facilitator** who builds **financial markets**, supports **smooth transmission**, meets **government financing needs** and promotes **socio-economic goals**.

**Recent events:** the **2008 global financial crisis** redefined mandates; the **Covid-19 pandemic** (a shock to **demand, supply and finance**) led central banks to use many measures to **support markets**.

items.title: Why and how central banks emerged
items.core_explanation_md:
**Main stimulus:** the **need to finance wars**. Many early central banks were set up (and later **nationalised**) for **war finance**; after war, they turned to **mobilising resources for development** and **fighting inflation**.

**First functions:** **lender of last resort** and **monopoly of note issue** (one issuer makes the **quantity, quality and acceptability** of currency controllable and protects the **internal value of money**). Central banks also took charge of the **external value of money** (the exchange rate) to support **trade**.

**Early history (as the courseware states):** **Riksbank (Sweden, 1668)** is treated as the **first central bank** (a joint stock bank lending to the Government; **note issue monopoly in 1897**); the **Bank of England** and **Banque de France** were set up with **private capital** and helped sovereigns **finance their debt**. Nineteenth century bank dates: **France 1800**, **Finland 1811**, **Netherlands 1814**, **Austria and Norway 1816**, **Denmark 1818**, **Portugal 1846**, **Belgium 1850**, **Spain 1874**, **Germany 1876**, **Italy 1893**, **Japan 1882**.

**Widening role:** developing the **financial system**, **payment and settlement systems** (central banks provide **finality of settlement**), then **regulation and supervision** after bank failures, plus **risk management**. In **developing countries** (including India) post-colonial mandates grew to **development**, raising the risk of **fiscal dominance**. From the late twentieth century **price stability, financial stability and risk management** came to the fore.
items.expanded_explanation_md: War finance explains why many central banks started as government bankers.

items.title: How the functions of central banks evolved
items.core_explanation_md:
**Milestones:** **paper money** issued by central banks replaced **full-value coins** around **World War I**; once notes were **legal tender** and **not convertible into gold**, central banks could control **money supply and prices**. After WWI they took on **supervision of commercial banks**, a firmer **lender of last resort** role, **credit to governments** and **debt management**, and used **open market operations** to fine-tune **interest rates and money supply**. Since **1933 (US)** and soon after **WWII (Germany)** central banks could impose **minimum reserve requirements**.

**Crises changed mandates:** the **Great Depression** added **monetary stability, full employment and growth**. Functions group into **monetary policy**, **banker to banks**, **banker to government** and **developmental** functions; **note issue and internal and external value of currency** are the key areas, with **growth promotion** added later.

**Financial stability** became an added objective, so **supervisory functions** grew; many central banks have **stopped financing their governments**.

**Moral hazard in last resort lending:** banks may behave **complacently** expecting **rescue**; central banks counter with **rigorous scrutiny** and by lending **at a penal rate**.

**Development role:** because **financial and economic development go together**, central banks run **credit policy**, **build institutions** and put in place **mechanisms to contain risks** from financial deepening.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Each crisis added a function: supervision after bank panics, reserve requirements after inflation, and stability after the 2008 crisis.

items.title: Reasons for proliferation and conflicting roles
items.core_explanation_md:
**Growth in number:** only about **a dozen** central banks in **1800**, but **over 160** now (courseware count). Reasons: **banking became complex**, **bank failures** made **regulation** necessary, and central banks **spread with nation states**.

**Why a central bank exists:** (1) an authority to run **note issue**; (2) an agency to be **banker and lender to the government**; (3) an agency to **regulate and supervise financial entities** and be **lender of last resort**.

**Conflicts of role:**

- **Banker or debt manager to Government vs price stability:** lending to the Government means **creating money**, risking **inflation**. This supports **central bank independence**, strengthened after the **Vietnam war** inflation and the **Latin American** episodes; **inflation targeting** (an **independent** bank pursuing a **target band**) became the main objective in many countries. A competing 'come of age' debate says central banks should not drop their 'parent', the **sovereign Government**.
- **Regulator and supervisor roles:** possible **conflict of interest**; by analogy with **Montesquieu's separation of powers** some countries moved supervision out of the central bank (the **UK Financial Services Authority, 2000**); in **India** the **Board for Financial Supervision** works **within the Reserve Bank**.

**Anchors:** price stability and the **external value** of currency relied on the **Gold Standard** and then the **dollar anchor**; the world lost its **anchor** on **15 August 1971** when the **US delinked the dollar from gold**.

**Modern core:** **development of financial markets and institutions**, **regulation and supervision**, **government debt management**, **payment and settlement systems** and the **external value** of currency; consensus that **inflation targeting** should be the **sole mandate** is **lacking**.

items.title: Central banks in developed and developing countries
items.core_explanation_md:
| Feature | Developed countries | Developing countries |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Financial structure** | **Diversified and strong**; both **widening and deepening** | **Poor infrastructure**, **sparse banking network** |
| **Transmission** | **Smooth and fast**; interest rate changes pass through quickly | **Weak**; **informal markets** do not respond to policy signals |
| **Payments** | Mostly **cheques and drafts**; **currency to deposit ratio below about 10 per cent** | **Currency dominates**; **ratio as high as 80 per cent** in some; currency management is complex |
| **Origin of central bank** | Mainly **lender of last resort** | To **promote spread of commercial banks and credit flow**: a **developmental role** |
| **Instruments** | **Market based** (for example the **federal funds rate** as operating target 1970-79) | More **direct, sector specific tools** at first; must **develop financial markets** |
| **Autonomy** | High | Often limited, with **fiscal dominance** |

**Old vs transition economies:** transition economies can **start on a clean slate** and **graft systems** from developed countries; older developing countries must fit new frameworks to **existing systems**; a model must be **tailored to country features**.

**Role in developing countries:** a **facilitator** who builds **financial markets**, supports **smooth transmission**, meets **government financing needs** and promotes **socio-economic goals**.

**Recent events:** the **2008 global financial crisis** redefined mandates; the **Covid-19 pandemic** (a shock to **demand, supply and finance**) led central banks to use many measures to **support markets**.
